newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada T-bills open weaker after strong U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Canada T-bills open weaker after strong U.S. data.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened weaker on Wednesday, softening in sympathy with U.S. fixed-income markets, which weakened on stronger-than-expected U.S. economic data, dealers said.

"After that strong (U.S) GDP number the market is basically going to have to change its stance. Yesterday there was some belief that the strong growth-inflation scenario was not really in place," said a T-bill trader with one bank-owned brokerage.
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.22 percent from 3.17 percent at Tuesday's close.

Both Canadian and U.S. fixed-income markets weakened following the U.S. report showing GDP grew at a greater than expected 5.6 percent in the first quarter. Another report showed Canada's monthly GDP data rose 0.5 percent in February, in line with some expectations.
The U.S. report had the largest impact, as it increased speculation that the U.S. Federal Reserve will hike interest rates in the near future.
"Certainly in May there's going to be a (Fed) move, 25 points at least. It's come back into the market, so we're trading off of that," the trader said.
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.62 percent from 3.55 percent on Tuesday. The one-year T-bill softened to yield 4.27 percent from 4.20 percent on Tuesday.

The call loan rate traded at 3.20 percent, in the upper half of the Bank of Canada's 2.75-3.25 percent target range. Dealers said the call loan rate was trading at higher than usual levels because of tax-related and month-end settlement pressures. One trader said the Bank of Canada would likely intervene on money market with specials to relieve pressure on the call loan rate.
